records.p: In males of the Purple-throated Sunbird, the violet-glossed throat contrasts with a reddish chest, dark maroon mantle and metallic green highlights toward the rump. The female was described as olive above with a yellow-green underside and a subtle warm tint along the flight-feather edges. Iridescent colours may look black in poor light, and these male marks do not apply to females (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Purple-throated Sunbird is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, Siargao, and Basilan, including Mainit Hot Spring Protected Landscape on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Purple-throated Sunbird is broadly associated with forests.

Bright golden-yellow plumage contrasts with a broad black band from the eyes across the nape and black flight feathers; bill is pinkish (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Black-naped Oriole has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, Siargao, and Basilan, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Black-naped Oriole is associated with forests. Eats fruits and insects in trees and occasionally joins groups feeding at fruiting trees (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

The Philippine Oriole’s Greater Mindanao populations were treated historically under several names, including Oriolus samarensis in the east and O. basilanicus in the west. Those museum birds were mostly olive-yellow above with a grey throat and breast, pale lower belly often showing thin dark shaft streaks, yellow undertail region and a reddish bill. McGregor reported regional differences in throat tone and streaking. The historical forms are now commonly treated within O. steerii, and the described markings must be interpreted geographically rather than as fixed traits of all populations (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Philippine Oriole has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Siargao, and Basilan, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). The Philippine Oriole is broadly associated with forests.

In McGregor’s historical Sulu specimen series, the upperparts were reddish brown with a darker crown, and the underparts were largely white with cinnamon markings on the throat, breast sides and flanks. These are original regional plumage descriptions, not a complete diagnosis of all populations now assigned to Pachycephala homeyeri (McGregor, 1909–1910). The White-vented Whistler has records from Mindanao, Samar, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Busa Mountain Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, and Sarangani. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). Historic notes describe insect feeding above ground level in wooded habitats of Tawi-Tawi and Sulu (McGregor, 1909–1910). The White-vented Whistler is associated with forests.

The Yellow-bellied Whistler has an olive-green upperbody, greyer crown and face, pale throat and bright yellow belly. Some named forms have more grey across the head and chest, while young birds can show warmer brown or rufous feathering. Because the color balance differs among island populations, the overall yellow ventral plumage is not sufficient to identify an unphotographed or poorly observed whistler to species (BirdForum Opus, n.d.). The Yellow-bellied Whistler has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Basilan, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Yellow-bellied Whistler is broadly associated with forests.

The Elegant Tit has yellow cheeks and underparts contrasted with a black cap, black throat bib and dark wings. Small whitish spots interrupt the wing, while white markings appear along the tips and sides of an otherwise dark tail. Females are generally less vivid. Cornell’s eBird treatment uses the genus Periparus for this species, whereas this manuscript follows Pardaliparus; the identification features refer to the same named bird (Cornell Lab of Ornithology, eBird, n.d.). The Elegant Tit is documented on Mindanao, Samar and Leyte. Reports from Bohol in aggregated occurrence data conflict with the 2025 WBCP range summary and remain unconfirmed (GBIF.org, 2026; WBCP, 2025). The Elegant Tit is associated with forests. Early observers recorded birds searching terminal foliage and sometimes hanging upside-down while feeding; breeding was noted on Cebu in June (McGregor, 1909–1910).

r.short: Cornell Lab of Ornithology, eBird, n.d.

records.p: A predominantly glossy black tit with a conspicuous white forehead and pale lores. Older Philippine treatments distinguished the Mindanao form by a broad white patch across the inner flight feathers, whereas other historical populations lacked a prominent white wing bar (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Mindanao taxon is now treated as Sittiparus semilarvatus nehrkorni; the historical names and comparative characters require this geographic qualification (ITIS, 2026). The White-fronted Tit has been documented on Mindanao, including Lituban–Quipit Watershed, Lake Lanao, Agusan del Sur, and Sultan Kudarat (GBIF.org, 2026). The White-fronted Tit is broadly associated with forests. AVONET lists a culmen length of 11.9 mm, wing length of 74.2 mm, tail length of 49.5 mm, and body mass of 18 g (Tobias et al., 2022). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

The Cinnamon Ibon has vivid cinnamon-rufous upperparts and pale buff underparts, becoming greyer toward the lower belly, with a relatively stout, slightly decurved bill. McGregor emphasized the absence of a conspicuous white eye ring in this bird despite its superficial resemblance to small olive forest passerines. Both sexes in the historical treatment were generally similar (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Cinnamon Ibon has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Matutum, and South Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Cinnamon Ibon is broadly associated with forests.

The brown crown, black cheek spot and black throat bib set it apart from several other small urban sparrows (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Eurasian Tree Sparrow is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Eurasian Tree Sparrow is associated with agricultural areas as well as settlements and disturbed habitats. The Eurasian Tree Sparrow usually gathers in flocks and feeds mainly on the ground, also visiting seeds on plants (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

The Mindanao Ground Babbler has a fulvous-brown crown and back, narrow black feather edging on the head and faint pale shaft-streaks on the back. Steere’s original comparative description separated it from the Basilan Ground Babbler by the more uniformly fulvous back and head rather than differences in overall size (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Striated Wren-Babbler has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Striated Wren-Babbler is broadly associated with forests.

Olive-brown upperparts, pale eyebrow, slender pale-based bill with dark lower tip and one or two narrow wing bars distinguish this leaf warbler (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Arctic Warbler has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). Moves actively through leaves, searching for insect prey, often high in the tree canopy (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

The Kamchatka Leaf Warbler belongs to the Arctic Warbler complex: olive-green above and pale below, with a pale eyebrow and wing-bars, it is extremely similar in appearance to both P. borealis and P. xanthodryas. Differences in colour and size overlap and cannot safely establish species from a normal field view. On the breeding grounds, its song is a comparatively short, rapid, regularly pulsing series, whereas calls are also distinctive from the two relatives; Philippine nonbreeding birds require suitably documented calls, or other direct diagnostic evidence, for confident assignment. Silent birds should remain unidentified within the complex (Alström et al., 2011; Perez, 2014). The Kamchatka Leaf Warbler is recorded on Mindanao and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Cinchona Forest Reserve, Zamboanga del Sur, and Davao del Sur. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Kamchatka Leaf Warbler is broadly associated with forests, freshwater wetlands, shrubland, and settlements and disturbed habitats. AVONET lists a culmen length of 13.5 mm, wing length of 66.2 mm, tail length of 47 mm, and body mass of 10.9 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

In the Mount Melibengoy population, photographed birds showed greenish-grey plumage and variable pale eye-rings, differing from descriptions of the usual olive-green upperparts, yellow underparts and less conspicuous eye-rings. The authors raised a taxonomic question rather than formally naming a new taxon (Pitogo et al., 2024). The Negros Leaf Warbler has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Mount Apo Natural Park, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Tagubud, and Misamis Occidental (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Negros Leaf Warbler is broadly associated with forests.

Du Pont’s Philippine bird monograph describes the Philippine Leaf Warbler as olive green above with a lighter rump and yellow supercilium. The chin and throat are whitish; the grey-white breast and belly show a yellow wash, and the undertail coverts are yellow. The upper bill is black and the lower mandible yellowish (du Pont, 1971). The Philippine Leaf Warbler is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Mount Capotoan on Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Philippine Leaf Warbler is broadly associated with forests.

records.p: The Japanese Leaf Warbler is an Arctic-type leaf warbler with a fine bill, pale eyebrow, olive-green upperparts and pale underparts. On average it is brighter green above and has more yellow on the throat and underside than Kamchatka or Arctic Warbler, but these plumage tendencies overlap. Its species status is supported by distinct songs and calls together with genetic and morphometric evidence. For Philippine field records, a suitably documented species-specific call is the strongest practical distinction; visual colour alone is insufficient, so silent or inadequately heard birds should remain unidentified within the Arctic Warbler complex (Alström et al., 2011; Perez, 2014). The Japanese Leaf Warbler is recorded on Mindanao and Bohol (GBIF.org, 2026). The Japanese Leaf Warbler is broadly associated with forests. AVONET lists a culmen length of 13.5 mm, wing length of 66.2 mm, tail length of 47 mm, and body mass of 10.9 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

Philippine Pitta accounts of the erythrogaster complex describe a striking combination of warm reddish head or face, darker throat, green-to-blue upperparts and a strong red lower belly. A contrasting cobalt-blue breast or mantle band occurs in some forms, and juveniles can be far duller and spotted. The source includes historical Blue-breasted and Sulu forms under a broader concept, so these plumage elements cannot be assigned indiscriminately to every current species or subspecies (BirdForum Opus, n.d.). The Philippine Pitta is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Cinchona Forest Reserve on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). The Philippine Pitta is broadly associated with forests.

The black facial band, green back, ultramarine wing coverts and ruddy belly with red vent identify the species (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Blue-winged Pitta is recorded on Mindanao (Avibase, 2026). The Blue-winged Pitta is broadly associated with forests.

The Hooded Pitta complex has a green body contrasted with a dark or black head, a blue shoulder patch and bright red undertail region. Some forms also have conspicuous pale markings in the wings. Juveniles are less brightly colored. Taxonomic treatments differ in how the Philippine and wider Asian populations are partitioned, so head color, wing patches and the relevant subspecies must be checked against the current adopted checklist (BirdForum Opus, n.d.). The Western Hooded Pitta has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Bohol, Siargao, and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park. On Leyte, records include Mount Nacolod and Southern Leyte. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Western Hooded Pitta is broadly associated with forests.

A white throat, metallic pale-blue belly, green upperparts, and bright red undertail distinguish adults (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Azure-breasted Pitta has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). The Azure-breasted Pitta inhabits lowland tropical forest, including limestone forest with dense understorey, and spends much of its time on the ground (BirdLife International, 2025). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

r.full: BirdLife International. (2025). Azure-breasted Pitta (Pitta steerii). The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species. https://doi.org/10.2305/IUCN.UK.2025-2.RLTS.T22698644A231732291.en

records.p: Adults described as olive-yellow above with dark flight and tail feathers edged olive-yellow. The yellow chin and adjacent jaw feathers have conspicuous dark, sometimes projecting shaft tips; the throat and upper breast are pale cinnamon-brown washed with yellow, becoming brighter yellow on the abdomen and undertail. Sexes were reported as similar. The old account used Iole everetti, and its character descriptions should not be transferred to Camiguin populations now treated separately (McGregor, 1910). The Yellowish Bulbul is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Apo Natural Park on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). The Yellowish Bulbul is broadly associated with forests.

The Philippine Bulbul has a brownish-grey crown with pale feather edges, a reddish-brown throat and breast with white streaks, and a greenish-brown body. The lower belly and undertail-coverts are pale with a yellowish wash, and the bill is black (WildAlert, n.d.). The Philippine Bulbul is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Philippine Bulbul is broadly associated with forests.

AVONET lists a culmen length of 27.7 mm, wing length of 114.3 mm, tail length of 99 mm, and body mass of 58.7 g (Tobias et al., 2022). The Zamboanga Bulbul has been documented on Mindanao and Basilan. On Mindanao, records include Mount Malindang Range, Lituban–Quipit Watershed, Pasonanca area, Lake Lanao, and Zamboanga del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Zamboanga Bulbul uses forest edges and secondary growth, including fruiting guava bushes (McGregor, 1909–1910). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

The Wattled Bulbul has a dark-brown crown, olive-green back, drab-grey throat, ash-brown breast and whitish belly. Its short pointed hind-crown crest, narrow yellow eye-wattle and distinct white tips on the tail feathers give useful external recognition marks. The published specimen series notes a slightly longer bill and larger tail-tip patches in Basilan birds (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Yellow-wattled Bulbul has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026). The Yellow-wattled Bulbul forages among fruiting trees in forest and occasionally more open country (McGregor, 1909–1910). AVONET lists a culmen length of 15.2 mm, wing length of 79 mm, tail length of 83.2 mm, and body mass of 24.8 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

Olive-brown upperparts, white face and throat, dark lores and a vivid yellow patch beneath the tail identify adults (National Parks Board, 2019). The Yellow-vented Bulbul has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, Siargao, and Basilan, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Yellow-vented Bulbul is associated with forests. The Yellow-vented Bulbul takes berries, small fruits, nectar and insects, feeding in shrubs and trees (National Parks Board, 2019). Historical field notes describe feeding around fruit trees and bushes in open and secondary-growth habitats; insects occurred in one specimen's diet (McGregor, 1909–1910).

A strong black breast band and black face contrast with the pale underside and broad fanned tail (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Philippine Pied Fantail has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Apo Natural Park, Pasonanca area, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Tagubud, and Davao del Norte. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Philippine Pied Fantail is broadly associated with forests. A historical clutch of two eggs was collected on Marinduque on 8 May 1888 (McGregor, 1909–1910).

The white eyebrow and dark head sharply contrast with the rich cinnamon body and wings (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Black-and-cinnamon Fantail has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Mount Balatukan, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Matutum, and Agusan del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Black-and-cinnamon Fantail is broadly associated with forests.

This small blue fantail has a markedly dark, nearly blackish crown contrasting with brighter verditer-blue plumage over the remaining upperparts. In the original Samar–Leyte–Bohol comparison, both sexes were described as brighter blue above but darker crowned than Mindanao/Basilan Rhipidura superciliaris, whose upperparts were more cobalt-toned. The original comparison is useful for recognizing the regional forms, but the historical account does not establish a modern age-independent identification key (McGregor, 1910). The Visayan Blue Fantail is recorded on Samar, Leyte, and Bohol. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park and Eastern Samar. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Visayan Blue Fantail is broadly associated with forests. AVONET lists a culmen length of 13.2 mm, wing length of 76.8 mm, tail length of 78 mm, and body mass of 13.1 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

The blue upperparts, conspicuous pale supercilium, and light belly identify this Mindanao fantail (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Mindanao Blue Fantail has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026). The Mindanao Blue Fantail inhabits deep forest; breeding was historically reported on Mindanao and Basilan in August (McGregor, 1909–1910).

The Sulphur-billed Nuthatch was described with deep blue upperparts, a small white mark before the eye, pale violet-buff underparts and a pale bill. Females were described as lacking the dark line through the eye present in males. These are historical external characters rather than a modern subspecies key (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Sulphur-billed Nuthatch has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Sulphur-billed Nuthatch is broadly associated with forests.

The Citrine Canary-flycatcher is a small flycatcher with a yellow face, throat and underparts contrasted against olive-brown or greenish-brown upperparts. The head and upper breast can look brighter than the back; at field range, overall yellow color alone is insufficient to distinguish it from other small insectivorous forest birds. This description follows a community-compiled species synopsis and requires an additional specimen-based differential account (BirdForum Opus, n.d.). The Citrine Canary-flycatcher has records from Mindanao, Leyte, and Bohol, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Mount Lobi Range on Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Citrine Canary-flycatcher is associated with forests.

AVONET lists a culmen length of 27.1 mm, wing length of 134 mm, tail length of 81.2 mm, and body mass of 116.3 g (Tobias et al., 2022). The Crested Myna has records from Mindanao, Leyte, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Apo, Agusan del Sur, and Davao del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Crested Myna is associated with grasslands and open country and settlements and disturbed areas.

AVONET lists a culmen length of 17.5 mm, wing length of 105.2 mm, tail length of 49 mm, and body mass of 28.8 g (Tobias et al., 2022). The Chestnut-cheeked Starling has been documented on Mindanao and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Agusan del Sur, and South Cotabato. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Chestnut-cheeked Starling is associated with forests.

The Mindanao form of the Short-tailed Starling, Aplonis minor todayensis, was described historically as Lamprocorax todayensis. Its plumage is dark and glossy, with purplish-blue reflections and a more violet-purple throat sheen than in the larger Philippine Glossy Starling. The wings and short tail are dull purplish-black, and the iris is ruby-red. McGregor reproduced measurements of the original female specimen, including a 95 mm wing and 59 mm tail, rather than a range-wide average (McGregor, 1909–1910; ITIS, n.d.). The Short-tailed Starling has records from Mindanao and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mainit Hot Spring Protected Landscape, Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Apo Natural Park, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Matutum, Mount Tagubud, and Davao del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Short-tailed Starling is broadly associated with forests.

Adults are glossy dark green-black with red eyes; juveniles are grey-brown above with striking dark streaks on a white underside (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Asian Glossy Starling has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mainit Hot Spring Protected Landscape on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Asian Glossy Starling is associated with forests. The Asian Glossy Starling feeds largely on fruits and also takes insects and nectar; communal roosts may contain very large aggregations (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

AVONET lists a culmen length of 22.8 mm, wing length of 118.6 mm, tail length of 145.9 mm, and body mass of 110 g (Tobias et al., 2022). The Apo Myna has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Balatukan, Mount Apo Natural Park, Mount Toloma, and Misamis Oriental (GBIF.org, 2026). The Apo Myna is associated with forests. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

The Stripe-sided Rhabdornis differs from some Philippine congeners in its relatively plain grey-brown or brown crown and nape rather than extensive white head streaking. Its upperparts have faint pale feather shafts, with narrow pale streaks on the wings, and the underparts are whitish with darker streaking along the sides (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Stripe-breasted Rhabdornis has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Mount Capotoan on Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Stripe-breasted Rhabdornis is associated with forests.

In the Greater Mindanao islands, the form historically called Rhabdornis minor has a brownish rather than greyish back and a comparatively short bill. It retains the white-streaked head and contrasting dark facial marks characteristic of the group. McGregor (1909–1910) used these traits to distinguish R. minor from R. mystacalis sensu stricto. Modern checklists place the former as R. mystacalis minor, so the older descriptions must be read at subspecies level (Avibase, 2026). The Stripe-headed Rhabdornis has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol, including Mount Apo Natural Park on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Stripe-headed Rhabdornis feeds in woodland and secondary vegetation and has been observed more frequently there than in deep forest (McGregor, 1909–1910).

The bare dark skin of the head contrasts with a pale gray body, black wings, and a white lower-breast area (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Coleto has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, Siargao, and Basilan, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Coleto is associated with forests. Early collectors recorded feeding on fruits and nesting in cavities of dead trees (McGregor, 1909–1910).

The male Red-billed Starling has a pale creamy head, grey mantle and underparts, black wings and tail, a red bill and orange legs. The white bases of the primaries form a visible patch in flight. Females are duller, with browner head and underparts and less contrast between the pale body and dark wings (Hong Kong Bird Watching Society, 2023). The Red-billed Starling is recorded on Dinagat (GBIF.org, 2026). The Red-billed Starling is associated with grasslands and open country, shrublands, cultivated areas, and settlements and disturbed areas. This broad classification does not indicate local habitat selection or breeding habitat. AVONET lists a culmen length of 26.8 mm, wing length of 120.6 mm, tail length of 71.8 mm, and body mass of 65 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

records.p: The Basilan Tit-Babbler has a black head and neck boldly streaked white, white lores, rusty tan-brown back and wings, and a pale throat and belly with dark-edged feathers. The flanks are warm buff. The original description reported little plumage difference between males and females (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Brown Tit-Babbler is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Brown Tit-Babbler moves through tangled vines in forest and secondary growth, sometimes several metres above the ground (McGregor, 1909–1910).

The Mindanao Island-Thrush is variable across the island populations grouped within this species. Cornell’s 2024 Clements update describes Mindanao forms as mainly blackish with a greyer hood, except for the chestnut-bellied katanglad form. The nominate Negros population is brown. The species account therefore requires attention to the bird’s island and subspecies rather than one uniform plumage description (Clements Checklist, 2024). The Mindanao Island Thrush has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Mount Apo Natural Park, Mount Tagubud, and Misamis Occidental (GBIF.org, 2026). The Mindanao Island Thrush is broadly associated with forests.

Adult males have a grey head, bold white eyebrow and cheek stripe, orange flanks and upper breast, and a white belly; females are browner (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Eyebrowed Thrush has records from Mindanao and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Tagubud, Lake Holon, and North Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). Visits fruiting trees and also searches for food on the ground (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Eyebrowed Thrush is associated with forests.

The adult Sunda Thrush has very dark brown upperparts, darker toward the head, with little or no pale eye-stripe. The chin and upper throat are whitish with narrow dark transverse bars; the chest is pale slate grey and the dark flank feathers show large contrasting white diamond-shaped centres. The underside of the wing is distinctively patterned, with axillaries white at the base and black toward their ends. This is a historical specimen description, including an old Mindanao record; it is not a modern voucher-verified separation from every Philippine Zoothera (Seebohm, reproduced in McGregor, 1910). The Sunda Thrush has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range (GBIF.org, 2026). The Sunda Thrush is associated with forests. AVONET lists a culmen length of 28.1 mm, wing length of 120.8 mm, tail length of 69.8 mm, and body mass of 90.5 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

The Mindanao Pygmy Babbler was described under Zosterornis plateni as an extremely small forest bird with olive-brown upperparts, a warmer reddish rump, a rusty face and throat, and light shaft streaks on the breast. Its dark facial and throat pattern contrasts with the pale streaks. The original generic combination is historical and modern generic assignment should be cross-checked (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Mindanao Pygmy Babbler has been documented on Mindanao and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Mount Apo Natural Park, Pasonanca area, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Matutum, Lake Lanao, and Agusan del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Mindanao Pygmy Babbler is broadly associated with forests and shrubland. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

The Visayan Pygmy Babbler was treated historically as Zosterornis pygmaeus. Its upperparts were olive-brown, with narrow pale shaft streaks on the crown; the grey throat and upper breast showed fine white streaks against a paler belly. The pattern differs from the warmer and more rufous face and rump in the older description of the Mindanao pygmy babbler, but generic placement requires review (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Visayan Pygmy Babbler is documented on Samar and Leyte. Bohol appears in aggregated occurrence data but not in the 2025 WBCP island-range summary, so that record requires corroboration (GBIF.org, 2026; WBCP, 2025). The Visayan Pygmy Babbler is associated with forests. AVONET lists a culmen length of 11.1 mm, wing length of 50 mm, tail length of 41.5 mm, and body mass of 8.7 g (Tobias et al., 2022). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

The Mindanao Heleia shows olive upperparts, a browner forehead and dark lores, with a pale buff-white throat and a dull yellow-green wash below. The historic treatment under Zosterops goodfellowi specifically noted that the bold white eye ring familiar from many white-eyes is absent. Geographic variation in forehead and lower-face colour was described from Mindanao specimens (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Mindanao Heleia has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Apo, Mount Matutum, Mount Mayo, and Misamis Occidental (Avibase, 2026, based on the Clements checklist). The Mindanao Heleia is broadly associated with forests. AVONET lists a culmen length of 15 mm, wing length of 65.9 mm, tail length of 49.5 mm, and body mass of 20 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

r.short: Avibase, 2026, based on the Clements checklist

records.p: The Rusty-crowned Babbler has a distinctly rufous crown and throat, brownish upperparts marked by pale shaft streaks and a light yellowish belly. McGregor noted white tips to some outer tail feathers. A combination of the rusty head, barred-looking upperparts and paler belly is a more useful starting point than any single isolated feature (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Rusty-crowned Babbler has been documented on Mindanao, including Pasonanca area, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Matutum, Lake Lanao, and Agusan del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). The Rusty-crowned Babbler is broadly associated with forests.

The Visayan Babbler has a blackish forehead and crown, a rusty patch behind the eye, a greyish back and a warm yellow-ochre throat bordered by a rufous cheek or malar mark. Its belly is pale. This historical description applies to birds recorded from Samar and Leyte and may not capture all current geographic forms or age classes (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Visayan Babbler has been documented on Samar and Bohol. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park, Mount Capotoan, and Eastern Samar. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Visayan Babbler inhabits deep forest on Samar and moves among the upper branches of the understorey (McGregor, 1909–1910). AVONET lists a culmen length of 15.1 mm, wing length of 64.5 mm, tail length of 57.9 mm, and body mass of 14.1 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

Everett’s White-eye shows olive-green upperparts, a conspicuous white ring around each eye and yellow on the throat and vent, with a greyer or duller central belly. Plumage and eye-ring shape overlap with other Southeast Asian white-eyes, and some mainland populations historically included under this name have been reassigned. The Philippine account needs explicit comparison with local Zosterops and the current checklist concept (BirdForum Opus, n.d.). The Everett's White-eye has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Apo Natural Park on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Everett's White-eye is broadly associated with forests, shrubland, and cultivated land.

A small yellow-olive white-eye with a conspicuous ring of white feathers surrounding each eye. The Cornell Lab’s Warbling White-eye account emphasizes this strongly marked eye-ring and yellow-olive plumage, characters useful for first recognition but not sufficient by themselves to separate every similar white-eye. Mindanao records are associated with the diuatae and vulcani forms in the checklist taxonomy (Cornell Lab of Ornithology, n.d.; Avibase, 2026). The Warbling White-eye has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Apo, Mount Tagubud, Lake Holon, and South Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Warbling White-eye is associated with forests.

The Lowland White-eye is a small, yellow-green passerine with a conspicuous white ring around each eye, yellow forehead and throat, greenish-yellow upperparts and paler grey-brown lower belly. Its short bill is dark, and the legs and feet are dark grey-brown (DENR WildALERT, n.d.). The Lowland White-eye has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Malindawag and Mount Matutum (GBIF.org, 2026). The Lowland White-eye is broadly associated with forests and shrubland. AVONET lists a culmen length of 13.1 mm, wing length of 52 mm, tail length of 40.5 mm, and body mass of 10 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

The long S-shaped neck and gape extending beyond the eye are diagnostic (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Great Egret is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Zamboanga del Sur, and Surigao del Sur. On Leyte, records include Mount Nacolod and Southern Leyte. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Great Egret stalks shallow water slowly and strikes at fish and aquatic invertebrates using its pointed bill (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Great Egret is associated with freshwater wetlands as well as riverbanks and shorelines.

Breeding adults develop orange-buff plumes on the head, neck and back (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). Outside the breeding season, the plumage is largely white, with a relatively short yellow bill and dark legs. Breeding birds develop rufous-buff plumes (NParks Singapore, 2026). The Eastern Cattle Egret has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, Siargao, and Basilan. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Pasonanca area, Mount Tagubud, Lake Lanao, and Surigao del Sur. On Samar, records include Eastern Samar. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Eastern Cattle Egret is associated with freshwater wetlands, rivers and streams, grasslands and other open areas, and agricultural areas. The Eastern Cattle Egret feeds in short vegetation in association with livestock and other grazing animals (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

The wholly white plumage and elongated breeding back plumes accompany long dark legs (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Medium Egret has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Lake Lanao, Surigao del Sur, and Agusan del Sur. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Medium Egret is broadly associated with freshwater wetlands, riverbanks and shorelines.

A chestnut neck with bold black longitudinal stripes distinguishes this heron (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). Rufous neck and breast are vertically striped in dark slate, with black crown plumes and long pointed scapular feathers (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Purple Heron has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Lake Lanao, Zamboanga del Sur, and Surigao del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Purple Heron is broadly associated with freshwater wetlands, riverbanks and shorelines.

In breeding plumage the head is pale yellow with white plumes, the breast cinnamon-rufous and the back dark slate; nonbreeding pond herons are extremely similar to congeners (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Javan Pond Heron has records from Mindanao, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Lituban–Quipit Watershed, Surigao del Sur, and Agusan del Sur. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Javan Pond Heron feeds on fish, frogs, insects and crustaceans around freshwater and wet fields (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Javan Pond Heron is associated with freshwater wetlands as well as riverbanks and shorelines.

Adult males have largely cinnamon-chestnut upperparts and buff underparts with dark neck streaking (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Cinnamon Bittern has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Lituban–Quipit Watershed. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Cinnamon Bittern is associated with freshwater wetlands, rivers and streams, grasslands and other open areas, and cultivated areas.

The species has warm chestnut upperparts marked by a contrasting dark cap and pale throat (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Von Schrenck's Bittern has been documented on Mindanao, including Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary (GBIF.org, 2026). The Von Schrenck's Bittern is broadly associated with forests, freshwater wetlands, rivers and streams, and coastal and intertidal habitats.

The dark slaty upperparts and streaked pale throat contrast with a prominent yellowish stripe along the side of the neck (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Black Bittern is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary. On Samar, records include Mount Capotoan (GBIF.org, 2026). The Black Bittern is broadly associated with freshwater wetlands, rivers and streams, grasslands and other open habitats, as well as cultivated land.

A small bittern with a black crown and back in males, rich buff underparts and contrasting pale wing panels (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Yellow Bittern is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary, Zamboanga del Sur, and Agusan del Sur. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Yellow Bittern is broadly associated with freshwater wetlands, rivers and streams, grasslands and other open habitats, as well as cultivated land.

A compact grey heron with black crown and rear head plumes, a narrow dark bill and yellowish-orange legs; young birds have spotted wing-coverts (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Little Heron has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Pasonanca area, Agusan del Sur, and South Cotabato. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Little Heron is associated with freshwater wetlands, rivers and streams, grasslands and other open areas, and cultivated areas. The IOC World Bird List treats Butorides atricapilla separately from B. striata following phylogenetic work. Older records published under B. striata may include more than one present-day species (IOC World Bird List, 2025–2026).

r.full: IOC World Bird List. (2025–2026). Species updates: Little Heron Butorides atricapilla. https://www.worldbirdnames.org/new/updates/species-updates/

records.p: Nonbreeding birds are white with a thick dark bill showing yellow at the base and greenish-yellow legs; breeding adults have head plumes and a mostly yellow bill (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Chinese Egret has records from Mindanao and Bohol (GBIF.org, 2026). The Chinese Egret feeds actively on intertidal mud, running, darting and making short flights as it pursues prey (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Chinese Egret is associated with freshwater wetlands, agricultural areas, and coastal and intertidal habitats. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

Nonbreeding adults show white plumage, black legs and contrasting yellow feet (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). Breeding birds develop two elongated nape plumes and fine dorsal plumes that curve beyond the tail (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Little Egret is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, Siargao, and Basilan. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Pasonanca area, Surigao del Sur, and Bukidnon. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Little Egret forages along sandy shorelines and around mangroves, often feeding alone (McGregor, 1909–1910).

This reef heron has dark slate and white plumage morphs, with rather short yellowish legs (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Pacific Reef Heron has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao (GBIF.org, 2026). The Pacific Reef Heron is broadly associated with coastal and intertidal habitats and marine waters.

The Japanese Night-Heron has a chestnut crown and short crest, a comparatively short stout bill with dark upper and yellowish lower mandibles, yellow eyes, and buff-brown neck and breast marked by darker streaking. The darker flight feathers end in conspicuous tawny rather than white tips. Compared with the Malayan Night-Heron, its chestnut crown, shorter crest and bill, and tawny primary tips are useful; younger birds are browner, more spotted and less chestnut-headed (HeronConservation, n.d.). The Japanese Night Heron has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range and Davao del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). Camera traps in Hyogo, Japan, recorded birds walking on the forest floor during daylight, apparently searching for terrestrial prey (Ornithological Society of Japan, 2023). The Japanese Night Heron is associated with forests, freshwater wetlands, rivers and streams. AVONET lists a culmen length of 49.4 mm, wing length of 256.8 mm, tail length of 93.2 mm, and body mass of 527 g (Tobias et al., 2022). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Endangered (EN).

r.full: Ornithological Society of Japan. (2023). The behaviour of Japanese Night Heron Gorsachius goisagi on Awaji Island, Japan, recorded by camera traps. Ornithological Science, 22(2), 161–168. https://doi.org/10.2326/osj.22.161

records.p: Chestnut-brown upperparts, a black crest and conspicuous black-and-white barred underwing distinguish the species (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Malayan Night Heron has been documented on Mindanao (GBIF.org, 2026). The Malayan Night Heron uses forest habitats and is also listed from riverside environments in the regional working checklist (NParks, 2019). Two eggs described in the early Philippine literature were pale bluish-white, with measurements of 45.7 × 35.5 and 48.2 × 35.5 mm (McGregor, 1909–1910). Pellet and stomach analyses from the Yaeyama Islands, Japan, identified land snails, spiders, freshwater crabs and insects among prey (Chinese Birds, 2011).

r.full: Chinese Birds. (2011). Dietary characteristics of the Malayan Night Heron (Gorsachius melanolophus) in the Yaeyama Islands, southern Japan. https://doi.org/10.5122/cbirds.2011.0015

records.p: The adult Rufous Night-Heron has a short, stout bill, grey-black crown, cinnamon to rufous-brown back and wings, and pale underparts. Breeding adults may carry two or three long pale head plumes. Immatures are brown with buff and white spots and streaking, and are less readily separated from other night-herons (HeronConservation, n.d.). The Nankeen Night Heron has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Nankeen Night Heron is broadly associated with freshwater wetlands, riverbanks and shorelines.

Adults have a black crown and back, gray wings, white underparts and long white nuchal plumes in breeding dress (McGregor, 1909–1910). Immatures differ markedly from adults in having a brown body with buff spotting and streaking (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Black-crowned Night Heron is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Pasonanca area and Davao del Norte. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Black-crowned Night Heron is associated with freshwater wetlands as well as riverbanks and shorelines. The Black-crowned Night Heron frequently feeds from dusk through nighttime, unlike most day-active herons (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

The Australian Pelican is a very large, mostly white pelican with extensive black on the flight feathers and tail, a long pale bill and an enormous throat pouch. Adults have grey legs, while immature birds show browner areas where adults are black. Bill length and breeding-season pouch colours vary with age and sex (Australian Museum, 2024). The Australian Pelican was photographed along the Sarangani Bay coast of southern Mindanao in 2016. The observation is treated as an exceptional visiting record (Sarenas, 2016). The Australian Pelican is associated with freshwater wetlands, rivers and streams, and coastal and intertidal habitats. AVONET lists a culmen length of 414.2 mm, wing length of 601.5 mm, tail length of 151.2 mm, and body mass of 5505 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

r.full: Sarenas, I. (2016, October 1). Photo of the month: Australian Pelican. Wild Bird Club of the Philippines. https://birdwatch.ph/2016/10/01/photo-of-the-month-australian-pelican/

records.p: The Spot-billed Pelican is a relatively small, greyish pelican with a long bill bearing distinctive dark bluish spots on its sides and often on the throat pouch. Adults have pale underparts, a brownish-grey crest on the hind head and a pinkish to yellowish bill. The spotted bill and pouch are more informative than overall body colour (University of Michigan Museum of Zoology, n.d.). The Spot-billed Pelican has historical reports from Mindanao, including broader accounts mentioning Davao Gulf and inland wetland areas. Its present occurrence in Greater Mindanao is unconfirmed (McGregor, 1909–1910; Figueroa, 2019). The Spot-billed Pelican uses large freshwater and brackish wetlands and sheltered coastal waters. Breeding colonies elsewhere in Asia nest in trees near wetlands, but the historical Philippine records do not establish breeding within Greater Mindanao (McCubbrey, n.d.). AVONET lists a culmen length of 334.2 mm, wing length of 562.8 mm, tail length of 173.5 mm, and body mass of 5011 g (Tobias et al., 2022). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

r.short: University of Michigan Museum of Zoology, n.d.

McCubbrey, A. (n.d.). Pelecanus philippensis (spot-billed pelican). Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan. https://animaldiversity.org/accounts/Pelecanus_philippensis/

records.p: A long, slender, downcurved bill and dark iridescent plumage distinguish this ibis; breeding adults become rich chestnut with green iridescence (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Glossy Ibis has been documented on Mindanao, including Zamboanga del Sur and Sultan Kudarat (GBIF.org, 2026). The Glossy Ibis wades in shallow water and probes soft mud for aquatic invertebrates (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Glossy Ibis is associated with freshwater wetlands as well as agricultural areas.

Adult White-tailed Tropicbirds are mainly white, with a bold black mask through the eye, a bright bill and two very long, slender white tail streamers. Juveniles lack the extended tail feathers and show dark bars on the upperparts. The black facial stripe and streamer colour help separate adults from Red-tailed Tropicbirds (Cornell Lab of Ornithology, n.d.). The White-tailed Tropicbird is listed among occasional birds recorded from Mindanao (Lepage, 2026). White-tailed Tropicbirds plunge into marine waters to take fish and squid; nesting occurs in sheltered rock cavities (National Audubon Society, n.d.). The White-tailed Tropicbird is associated with offshore waters. AVONET lists a culmen length of 54.7 mm, wing length of 269.4 mm, tail length of 108.2 mm, and body mass of 328 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

Adult Red-tailed Tropicbirds are nearly all white, with a strong coral-red bill, little black around the eye and two long, narrow red tail streamers. The upper wings lack the extensive black marking seen in other tropicbirds. Juveniles have a dark bill, heavy black barring above and no long tail streamers (Cornell Lab of Ornithology, n.d.). The Red-tailed Tropicbird is recorded in the Zamboanga Peninsula of western Mindanao (Avibase, 2026). Red-tailed Tropicbirds feed at sea on small fish and squid and lay a single egg in sheltered ground or rock crevices (Cornell Lab of Ornithology, n.d.). The Red-tailed Tropicbird is associated with offshore waters. AVONET lists a culmen length of 70.8 mm, wing length of 330.5 mm, tail length of 99.8 mm, and body mass of 671.9 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

The Coppersmith Barbet is a small, green-backed barbet with a heavy bill, a red forehead and a red patch on the upper breast, separated by yellow on the face and throat. A black stripe crosses the eye and dark streaks mark the pale underparts. Young birds are duller and lack the conspicuous red patches of adults (National Parks Board Singapore, 2026). The Coppersmith Barbet has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Coppersmith Barbet is broadly associated with forests.

Males show a scarlet crown and rump with golden-yellow wing coverts; females have more olive-spotted crown feathers (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Buff-spotted Flameback has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Mount Capotoan on Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Buff-spotted Flameback has been recorded in both forest and secondary vegetation on Mindanao and Basilan (McGregor, 1909–1910).

A full scarlet crest, mostly black body and pale abdomen characterize adults; males also show red on the forehead and cheeks (McGregor, 1909–1910). The White-bellied Woodpecker has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). Ants were recorded as food in specimen notes attributed to Bourns and Worcester (McGregor, 1909–1910). The White-bellied Woodpecker is associated with forests.

A slaty-gray body, pale spots on the neck and scarlet cheek patch in males characterize this large woodpecker (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Southern Sooty Woodpecker has been documented on Mindanao and Samar. On Mindanao, records include Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary, Pasonanca area, Zamboanga del Sur, and Agusan del Sur. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026). The Southern Sooty Woodpecker is broadly associated with forests and settlements and disturbed habitats.

A small pied woodpecker with a broad pale stripe running from above the eye towards the nape, barred dark and pale upperparts and streaked or spotted underparts. Adult males bear a narrow red patch behind either side of the crown, lacking in females. Birds from Samar, Leyte and Bohol formerly called Yungipicus leytensis were described with a conspicuously white, faintly buff-washed rump. The Mindanao and Basilan form formerly called Y. fulvifasciatus had a pale buff back and rump and warmer yellowish underparts, often with comparatively smaller breast spots. These separate historical names are treated here only as insular forms within the checklist account; they do not define universal marks for all Y. maculatus (McGregor, 1909). The Philippine Pygmy Woodpecker is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Philippine Pygmy Woodpecker is associated with forests.

The male Tweeddale’s Frogmouth has rufous-brown plumage finely mottled and barred with dark brown, a narrow pale band across the mantle and two pale bands across the chest. White-tipped scapular and wing-covert feathers carry nearby dark spots. The female is less rufous and has a less sharply defined collar. McGregor distinguished it from the Javan Frogmouth by its greater size and comparatively shorter tail (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Philippine Frogmouth is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Philippine Frogmouth is broadly associated with forests.

A small diving waterbird with a short bill and rounded body; breeding birds have chestnut face and neck and a pale patch at the bill base (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Little Grebe has records from Mindanao, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Ligawasan Marsh, Lake Lanao, and Lanao del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Little Grebe dives rather than flying when disturbed and captures aquatic invertebrates and small fish under water (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Little Grebe is associated with freshwater wetlands.

The Wedge-tailed Shearwater is a long-winged shearwater with a pointed, wedge-shaped tail and an elongated dark bill. It occurs in both dark and pale morphs: dark birds are brown overall, whereas pale birds have grey-brown upperparts and a much paler underside. The wedge-shaped tail is more useful than colour alone for separating it from similarly dark shearwaters (Cornell Lab of Ornithology, n.d.). The Wedge-tailed Shearwater is recorded on Mindanao (GBIF.org, 2026). The Wedge-tailed Shearwater is broadly associated with coastal and intertidal habitats and marine waters. AVONET lists a culmen length of 40.9 mm, wing length of 296.8 mm, tail length of 130.4 mm, and body mass of 388 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

Bulwer’s Petrel is a slim, uniformly dark-brown petrel with unusually long pointed wings and a tapered, graduated tail. A buff diagonal bar crosses the upper side of each wing near the carpal region. In flight it typically follows the sea surface closely, with short bursts of wingbeats alternating with low twisting glides. The combination of long tapering tail and upperwing bars is more useful than overall dark coloration alone (Cornell Lab of Ornithology, n.d.). The Bulwer's Petrel is recorded in the Zamboanga Peninsula of western Mindanao (Avibase, 2026). The Bulwer's Petrel is broadly associated with coastal and intertidal habitats and marine waters. AVONET lists a culmen length of 21.6 mm, wing length of 203.2 mm, tail length of 110.8 mm, and body mass of 99 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

The Streaked Shearwater is a large shearwater, brown above and white below, with a mottled or streaked brown-and-white head and a relatively pale, long bill. In flight its long wings are often held slightly bowed and its pale underwing contrasts with the dark outer flight-feather tips and some dusky underwing markings (Hong Kong Bird Watching Society, n.d.). The Streaked Shearwater is recorded in the Zamboanga Peninsula of western Mindanao (Avibase, 2026). The Streaked Shearwater is associated with coastal and intertidal habitats as well as marine waters. The classification does not distinguish offshore foraging, coastal resting sites, or any local nesting evidence. AVONET lists a culmen length of 48.9 mm, wing length of 319.2 mm, tail length of 131.8 mm, and body mass of 580 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

r.short: Hong Kong Bird Watching Society, n.d.

records.p: The Red-vented Cockatoo is predominantly white, approximately 30–31 cm long, with a short erectile crest and a pale grey bill. Red undertail coverts and the yellowish underside of the tail are useful field marks (Philippine Department of Environment and Natural Resources, n.d.). The Red-vented Cockatoo is recorded on Mindanao, Bohol, and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range and Lake Lanao. On Leyte, records include Mount Nacolod and Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Red-vented Cockatoo is associated with lowland forest, mangroves and coastal woodland. Elsewhere in the Philippines, it nests in tree cavities and forages in forest and nearby open habitats (Philippine Cockatoo Conservation Programme / Katala Foundation, 2017; Widdman, 2001; McGregor, 1909–1910). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Critically Endangered (CR).

records.p: A compact, mostly yellow-green parrot with a short tail and contrasting blue on the face and throat. In the Mindanao form mindanensis, males have green cheeks separating the blue around the eyes from the blue throat and show a stronger blue collar. Females have a more yellow-green head and less extensive blue facial colour (World Parrot Trust, n.d.). The Guaiabero is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol, including Mainit Hot Spring Protected Landscape on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Guaiabero is associated with forest in the regional working checklist, which also includes karst landscapes among its broad habitat categories.

The Philippine Hanging Parrot is small and predominantly green, with a vivid red rump. In the southern Philippine apicalis form, males have a red crown grading toward orange on the nape, whereas females show pale-blue markings around the face and throat. The related Basilan dohertyi form has a stronger orange wash on the mantle (World Parrot Trust, n.d.). The Philippine Hanging Parrot is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Philippine Hanging Parrot forages in trees, including within the Hijo Forest survey area (Gamalo et al., 2023). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Critically Endangered (CR).

Adult Blue-crowned Racket-tails are mainly green, with a deep-blue crown extending toward the nape and elongated central tail shafts ending in dark, paddle-shaped racquets. The Mindanao discurus form has particularly extensive blue on the crown; juvenile birds may lack both the strong crown colour and the fully elongated tail feathers (World Parrot Trust, n.d.). The Blue-crowned Racket-tail is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Basilan, including Lituban–Quipit Watershed on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). The Blue-crowned Racket-tail feeds in fruiting trees in forest and sometimes mangroves, and calls while flying between trees (McGregor, 1909–1910). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

The Mindanao Racket-tail has a mainly green body with brown-washed upperparts, an olive-green underside and pale blue on the forehead and around the eyes. The elongated central tail feathers terminate in black racquets. Unlike the Blue-crowned Racket-tail, the blue is concentrated around the face rather than forming an extensive deep-blue crown; juveniles lack the fully formed tail racquets (World Parrot Trust, n.d.). The Mindanao Racket-tail has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Mount Apo Natural Park, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Tagubud, Mount Toloma, and South Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Mindanao Racket-tail is broadly associated with forests. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

records.p: The Mindanao Lorikeet is predominantly green with pink-red colouring across the forecrown and cheeks, a dark purplish stripe running from the lores toward the nape, and yellow underparts edged in green. Juveniles have less red on the face and a dusky bill rather than the adults’ orange-red bill (World Parrot Trust, n.d.). The Mindanao Lorikeet has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Mount Balatukan, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Matutum, Lake Lanao, and Misamis Oriental (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Mindanao Lorikeet inhabits old-growth montane forest. Records from Mount Melibengoy include forest both inside and beyond the protected boundary (Pitogo et al., 2024). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

Bright blue crown, green body, multicolored blue-and-gold upperwing, and red upper mandible distinguish adults (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Blue-naped Parrot has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Basilan. On Mindanao, records include Pasonanca area, Mount Matutum, and Cotabato. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park. On Leyte, records include Mount Lobi Range, Mount Nacolod, and Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Blue-naped Parrot is associated with forests. Nesting was reported in natural holes and abandoned woodpecker cavities in dead trees (McGregor, 1909–1910). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Critically Endangered (CR).

The exceptionally deep robust red bill and green head distinguish this large parrot from smaller related species (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Great-billed Parrot has records from Mindanao (GBIF.org, 2026). The Great-billed Parrot is broadly associated with forests and coastal and intertidal habitats.

AVONET lists a culmen length of 27.3 mm, wing length of 297.2 mm, tail length of 146.5 mm, and body mass of 322.6 g (Tobias et al., 2022). The Short-eared Owl appears in historical Philippine wildlife records that include Mindanao. Regular occurrence on the island has not been established (DENR-PAWB, 2004). The Short-eared Owl is associated with forests, freshwater wetlands, grasslands and other open areas, and coastal and intertidal habitats.

AVONET lists comparative values under the older name Bubo philippensis: culmen 47.5 mm, wing 341.2 mm, tarsus 67.5 mm and body mass 532.5 g (Tobias et al., 2022). The Philippine Eagle-Owl has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Lituban–Quipit Watershed, and Busa Mountain Range. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026). The Philippine Eagle-Owl is broadly associated with forests. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Endangered (EN).

A brown owl with large yellow eyes and pale underparts marked by relatively narrow, elongated teardrop-shaped brown spots (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Northern Boobook has been documented on Mindanao and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Tagubud, Zamboanga del Sur, and Davao de Oro. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Northern Boobook is associated with forests. The Northern Boobook hunts at night from perches, striking prey on the ground or in foliage (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

The Chocolate Boobook has rich reddish-chocolate brown upperparts, with the crown close in colour to the mantle. Its tail shows reddish-brown bands, and its underside carries more chestnut than white. In the original description under Ninox scutulata randi, Deignan (1951) distinguished its particularly stout bill and enlarged toes and claws from the related migrant form. The differences were based on museum skins under historical species limits. The Chocolate Boobook has records from Mindanao and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Pasonanca area, Mount Tagubud, Lake Holon, Surigao del Sur, and Agusan del Sur. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Chocolate Boobook is broadly associated with montane environments. AVONET lists a culmen length of 26.4 mm, wing length of 226 mm, tail length of 114 mm, and body mass of 202 g (Tobias et al., 2022). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

Compared with Northern Boobook, the dark marks on its pale underside are broader and heart-shaped; both have yellow eyes and brown plumage (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Brown Boobook has a small number of reports from Mindanao and Samar in aggregated records. The 2025 WBCP range summary emphasizes Palawan, whereas the 2026 Avibase Mindanao checklist includes the species, so these records should be regarded as exceptional pending confirmation (GBIF.org, 2026; WBCP, 2025; Avibase, 2026). The Brown Boobook is associated with forests, freshwater wetlands, and coastal and intertidal habitats. The Brown Boobook hunts from perches at dusk and during the night, and pairs may call in duet (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

The Mindanao Boobook has a spotted crown, a breast with irregular dark barring and mottling, and a paler belly marked by longitudinal dark streaks. Long, conspicuous ear-covert extensions and a low-pitched, mellow two-noted song help distinguish it from other Philippine boobooks (Rasmussen et al., 2012). The Mindanao Boobook has been documented on Mindanao, Siargao, and Basilan. On Mindanao, records include Cinchona Forest Reserve, Pasonanca area, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Lake Holon, and Agusan del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026). Historical records describe daytime concealment among dense vines and bushes; beetles and grasshoppers were recorded as prey (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Mindanao Boobook is associated with forests. AVONET lists a culmen length of 24.5 mm, wing length of 177.5 mm, tail length of 82.1 mm, and body mass of 137 g (Tobias et al., 2022). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

An ear-tufted scops owl with dark rich-brown upperparts, a pale forehead and superciliary stripes continuing around the nape, and a dark postocular stripe extending into the ear tufts. The lower plumage is ruddier brown with irregular dark markings rather than regularly barred abdominal feathers in the historical comparison. These are Tweeddale’s specimen-based characters, not a verified modern key to every Philippine Otus (Tweeddale, 1878, reproduced in McGregor, 1909). The Everett's Scops Owl has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Everett's Scops Owl is broadly associated with forests.

The Giant Scops Owl is a comparatively large scops owl with well-developed ear tufts, dark eyes and a rufous facial disc edged by contrasting dark and pale feathers. The underparts are warm buff to rufous, marked with strong dark longitudinal streaks. Its size and facial pattern help separate it from smaller Philippine scops owls, but an observation requires comparison with geographic congeners and variation in age and plumage (BirdLife International, 2017). The Giant Scops Owl is recorded on Mindanao and Samar. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Kitanglad Range, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Lindasan, Mount Pasian, Lake Lanao, and Davao del Norte. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Giant Scops Owl is associated with forests. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Endangered (EN).

This small scops owl was historically distinguished from the Luzon Scops Owl under the name Otus scops mirus. The Mindanao specimens were described as having more heavily streaked upperparts, a lighter belly and a smaller size than the comparative Luzon form. These are comparative museum characters, and poorly seen owls require vocal and contextual evidence (duPont, 1971, summarizing Ripley and Rabor’s 1968 description). The Mindanao Scops Owl has been documented on Mindanao, including Mainit Hot Spring Protected Landscape, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Apo, Mount Tagubud, and North Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). The Mindanao Scops Owl is broadly associated with forests.
